title: Organizational change management: current state to target state
blurb: Define OCM, explain how the change management approach moves an organization from its current state to a target state, and where culture fits.
question: A utility is piloting agile ways of working in one project. Which PRINCE2 product should describe the move from today's ways of working to the new ones, and what is OCM?

teach.h: OCM: getting from here to there
teach.body: Organizational change management (OCM) is the means by which an organization transitions from its current state to its target state. In plain English: a project can deliver new products, but benefits only appear when people actually change how they work. OCM is the discipline that plans and leads that shift, step by step, so the new way of working is adopted and stays in place.

teach.h: From current state to target state

steps.label: Interim state 1
steps.sub: For example, one pilot team works in iterations

steps.label: Target state
steps.sub: New ways of working adopted and kept

teach.caption: The change management approach can describe each state and how the business moves through them.

teach.body: PRINCE2 Project Management recommends that a project has a change management approach, and it can be tailored for use outside a project. In PRINCE2 Agile it can define the target organizational state for introducing the agile mindset and values, together with how the business will shift from the current state through any interim states. It is agreed in initiating a project, alongside the other management approaches.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 4.2.1, Table 4.1; Table 13.6

teach.h: Deciding how much detail to capture
head: Consider
Why it matters
rows: People need to know what is changing and why
New ways of working need new skills
Culture decides whether change is adopted
Change must still hold after the project
teach.caption: Examples given in book 4.2.1. PRINCE2 7 also lists impacted areas, key relationships and skills during and after transition.

teach.h: Which product describes an agile change?

root.label: How wide is the agile adoption?

children.label: An agile transformation plan, which can replace it

teach.h: Agile transformation plan versus change management approach
teach.body: An agile transformation plan guides an initiative to adopt (more) agility. It holds high-level goals aligning new target states to organizational strategy, plus short-term objectives for practical implementation, and typically spans several projects. For a single pilot it may not be needed yet: update the change management approach instead. In the project initiation workshop, the agile transformation plan can replace the change management approach if needed.

Northmoor Water is piloting agile in one project to rebuild its customer billing portal. Project manager Priya Venkatesan does not write a separate agile transformation plan for a single pilot. Instead, in initiating a project, she updates the change management approach: the current state (annual releases, sign-off by committee), an interim state (one team working in two-week iterations) and the target state (billing teams prioritizing with users). She adds how the new habits will be kept once the project closes.

teach.text: Do not mix up three things. OCM is the discipline of moving from current to target state. The change management approach is the PRINCE2 product that describes that move for the project. The agile transformation plan covers adopting agility across several initiatives. None of them is change control, which handles baseline changes in the issues practice.

items: OCM: how an organization transitions from its current state to its target state (4.2.1).
The change management approach defines the target state and the route through interim states.
It can be tailored for use outside a project and is agreed in initiating a project.
Consider communication, upskilling, the evolving culture and stopping changes rolling back.
A single pilot updates the change management approach; wider adoption uses an agile transformation plan.
OCM is not change control (issues practice).

summary: You can now define OCM as moving an organization from its current state to its target state, and explain what the change management approach describes. You can also tell it apart from the agile transformation plan and from change control.

options: The procedure for controlling changes to the project backlog baseline
How an organization moves from its current state to a target state
Applying methods, tools and techniques so a project meets its objectives
A plan of high-level goals for adopting agility across many initiatives
A.why: OCM is the means by which an organization transitions from the current state to the target state (book 4.2.1).

whyNot.0: Controlling baseline changes is change control in the issues practice.
whyNot.2: That describes project management, not OCM.
whyNot.3: That describes an agile transformation plan (2.7.1).

A.q: Which management product can define the target organizational state and how the business moves to it from the current state?
options: Communication management approach
Issue management approach
Benefits management approach
Change management approach
A.why: The change management approach can define the target organizational state and how the business shifts from the current state through any interim states (4.2.1, Table 4.1).

whyNot.0: The communication management approach covers the means and frequency of communication and feedback.
whyNot.1: The issue management approach covers how issues and baseline changes are handled.
whyNot.2: The benefits management approach covers benefits management actions and reviews.

A.q: When deciding how much detail to put in the change management approach, which consideration MOST helps the change last after the transformation?
options: The evolving culture and ways to stop changes rolling back
A bonus scheme that rewards people who adopt the change early
A detailed schedule of stage boundaries and tolerances
A rollout plan for the new agile planning software
A.why: Book 4.2.1 lists the evolving culture and ways to ensure changes are not rolled back after the transformation as a consideration; culture is what makes change stick.

whyNot.1: Financial incentives alone cannot guarantee that changes stay in place.
whyNot.2: Stage boundaries and tolerances are project controls, not what keeps a change embedded.
whyNot.3: Tools support a change but do not make the new ways of working stick.

B.q:
Which two statements about the change management approach are correct?
1. It can be tailored for use outside a project environment.
2. It handles requests to change the project backlog baseline.
3. It can describe the move from the current state through any interim states.
4. It is first produced in closing a project.
options: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: The change management approach can be tailored for use outside a project, and it describes how the business shifts from the current state through interim states to the target state (4.2.1).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is wrong: baseline changes are handled through the issues practice.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: baseline changes are an issues matter, and the approach is agreed in initiating a project.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the approach is agreed in initiating a project, not closing it.

B.q: A single pilot project is trialling agile ways of working in one department. What should normally describe the intended change in ways of working?
options: A new agile transformation plan for the department
An updated change management approach
An entry recorded in the issue register
The project product description
B.why: For a single pilot, an agile transformation plan may not be needed yet; the change management approach is updated instead (2.7.1).

whyNot.0: An agile transformation plan typically spans several projects or initiatives.
whyNot.2: The issue register records issues, not the planned organizational change.
whyNot.3: In PRINCE2 Agile the project product description is tailored into the project backlog; it describes products, not ways of working.

B.q: In which workshop can the agile transformation plan replace the change management approach, if needed?
options: Project kickoff workshop
Release planning workshop
Project initiation workshop
Team retrospective workshop
B.why: The management approaches topic of the project initiation workshop notes that the agile transformation plan can replace the change management approach if needed (Table 13.7).

whyNot.0: The kickoff workshop builds teamwork, team values, skill and delegation matrices and dashboards.
whyNot.1: The release planning workshop plans the next stage and updates the release map.
whyNot.3: The team retrospective workshop improves how one team works, in managing product delivery.

C.q: A transformation lead says OCM and change control are the same thing. Which statement corrects this?
options: OCM is change control carried out at the level of the project board
Change control is the part of OCM used for interim states
OCM moves the organization; change control handles baseline changes
OCM is the issue procedure used once a project has closed
C.why: OCM moves an organization from its current to its target state (4.2.1); change control deals with changes to baselines in the issues practice.

whyNot.0: OCM is not change control at any level; it is about people and ways of working.
whyNot.1: Interim states are part of the change management approach, not change control.
whyNot.3: OCM is not an issue procedure, and it runs during the project as well as after it.

C.q: How does an agile transformation plan differ from a change management approach?
options: It is the issue procedure used for agile change requests and swaps
It is produced by the team coach for one delivery team
It replaces the project canvas in starting up a project
It aligns target states to strategy across several initiatives
C.why: An agile transformation plan contains high-level goals aligning new target states to organizational strategy and typically spans several projects or initiatives (2.7.1).

whyNot.0: Agile change requests are handled through the issues practice.
whyNot.1: The team coach works with one or two teams; a transformation plan is organization-level.
whyNot.2: The project canvas is the agile form of the business case; the transformation plan does not replace it.

C.q: Which management approach records the target organizational state, and in which process is it agreed?
options: Change management approach, in initiating a project
Communication management approach, in starting up a project
Change management approach, in closing a project
Issue management approach, in managing a stage boundary
C.why: The change management approach describes the target state (4.2.1) and is agreed in the 'agree the management approaches' activity of initiating a project (Table 13.6).

whyNot.1: The communication management approach covers communication, and approaches are agreed in initiating, not starting up.
whyNot.2: The right product, but it is agreed in initiating a project, not at closure.
whyNot.3: The issue management approach handles issues, and approaches are agreed in initiating a project.

reteach.title: Moving house, not just buying furniture
reteach.question: If a family buys new furniture but never moves out of the old flat, have they moved house?

blocks.body: A project can deliver the furniture: new systems, new processes, new artifacts. OCM is the move itself: packing up the old habits, perhaps living in a temporary place for a while (interim states), and settling into the new home (target state) so that nobody drifts back. The change management approach is the moving plan.

blocks.text: Change control is about altering an agreed baseline (like swapping one sofa for another). OCM is about the whole household moving. Different ideas, different PRINCE2 products.

explain.body: OCM is the means by which an organization transitions from the current state to the target state (book 4.2.1).

options: one stage boundary to the next
its current state to a target state
a team plan to a stage plan
a risk register to an issue register
test.why: OCM is the means by which an organization transitions from the current state to the target state (4.2.1).

whyNot.0: Moving between stages is managing a stage boundary, not OCM.
whyNot.2: Team and stage plans are planning levels, not organizational states.
whyNot.3: Registers record risks and issues; they are not states of the organization.

explain.body: The change management approach can describe how the business shifts from the current state through any interim states to the target state. Big changes rarely happen in one jump.

test.q: Between the current state and the target state, the change management approach can describe:
options: any exception plans
the team skill matrix
any interim states
the product backlog
test.why: The change management approach describes how the business moves from the current state through any interim states (4.2.1, Table 4.1).

whyNot.0: Exception plans replace a plan when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded.
whyNot.1: The team skill matrix maps team skills; it is a technique of the organization practice.
whyNot.3: The product backlog holds a team's user stories.

explain.body: Book 4.2.1 asks you to consider the evolving culture and ways to ensure changes are not rolled back after the transformation. A change that fades once the project ends delivers little.

test.q: Which consideration helps ensure changes are not rolled back after a transformation?
options: Raising the time tolerance
Adding an extra stage boundary
Issuing a single launch announcement
Planning how the culture evolves
test.why: Book 4.2.1 links the evolving culture with ensuring changes are not rolled back after the transformation.

whyNot.0: Time tolerance is a progress control; it does not embed new ways of working.
whyNot.1: Stage boundaries are management control points, not a way to embed culture.
whyNot.2: One announcement does not change how people actually work.

explain.body: A single pilot updates the change management approach. Adopting agility across several initiatives calls for an agile transformation plan, which can replace the change management approach if needed.

test.q: For a single agile pilot project, an agile transformation plan:
options: may not be needed; update the change management approach
must be approved by the senior supplier before initiation
replaces the project canvas in starting up a project
is written by the team coach at each retrospective
test.why: For a single pilot the agile transformation plan may not be needed yet; the change management approach is updated instead (2.7.1).

whyNot.1: The senior supplier provides supplier resources; this is not a required approval for a pilot.
whyNot.2: The project canvas is the business case artifact; the transformation plan does not replace it.
whyNot.3: Retrospectives improve team working; they do not produce a transformation plan.
